title: Quentin and the Postcards
premise: Wendell Thornbury, a night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, discovers a box of undelivered postcards hidden behind a wardrobe in the condemned Thornbury family house — postcards written over forty years by her estranged uncle Quentin, each one addressed to someone who never received it. As she traces the intended recipients across the city, she uncovers how the family's patriarch buried a crime and arranged every inheritance, marriage, and silence around keeping it buried. Quentin, now dying in a care home, has been mailing copies of the postcards to strangers for years, waiting for one person to finally read them aloud. Wendell must choose between the justice the law can offer and the truth the family will pay anything to suppress, ending with her reading the final postcard at his deathbed as the house comes down around the secret.
about_author: Jude Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed correspondence in municipal storage. Their fiction explores what institutions keep and what people cannot say.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A night shift at the Halcyon Branch Library; we learn her habit of recording overheard confessions in a ledger she calls the inventory. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as order.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. She is sent to appraise books in the condemned Thornbury house before demolition and finds a box of undelivered postcards wedged behind a wardrobe, all in the same careful hand. Beat: curiosity sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: Quentin
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. The handwriting matches a name from her childhood — Uncle Quentin, erased from family talk. She reads three postcards and learns the first was addressed to a woman who died believing herself forgotten. Beat: grief arriving late.

chapters.title: Forty Years of Stamps
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. At home she sorts the postcards chronologically and realizes they were never mailed — until recently, when someone began sending duplicates to strangers. Beat: the sense of being summoned.

chapters.title: The First Recipient
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. She tracks down Marisol Vega, whose mother received a postcard last spring. Marisol reveals her mother spent her final months convinced an old debt would be repaid. Beat: the past pressing into the present.

chapters.title: What the Family Arranged
chapters.summary: POV shift to Quentin, decades earlier. A young Quentin witnesses his father Aldous settle a worker's death on the docks with money and silence, then dictate the terms of everyone's loyalty. Beat: the birth of a dynasty's quiet rot.

chapters.title: A Visit Refused
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. She visits the Thornbury estate and is turned away by her cousin Ambrose, who knows exactly why she came and offers her money instead. Beat: temptation wearing a polite face.

chapters.title: The Ledger and the Box
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. She begins entering the postcards into her library inventory, treating them like catalogued evidence, and notices dates that contradict the official family history. Beat: method as resistance.

chapters.title: The Docks, 1979
chapters.summary: Quentin POV. The night Renny Okafor died under a collapsed crane; Aldous burns the safety reports while Quentin holds the match he was told not to light. Beat: complicity as inheritance.

chapters.title: Marisol's Mother's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Marisol POV. She shows Wendell her mother's notebook, which mirrors the postcards' contents — two strangers documenting the same crime from opposite sides. Beat: converging truths.

chapters.title: Ambrose Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Ambrose POV. He calculates what the postcards could cost the family trust and decides Wendell is a problem to be managed, not a relative to be loved. Beat: corruption as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: The Care Home on Fenwick Road
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. She finds Quentin alive, frail, and unrepentant about the mailings: 'Someone had to keep sending the truth until somebody opened it.' Beat: meeting the author of your wound.

chapters.title: Why He Never Sent Them
chapters.summary: Quentin POV. He explains the original cowardice — forty years of addressed but unmailed postcards, courage deferred annually. Beat: pity entangled with anger.

chapters.title: The Library Closes Early
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Her supervisor, pressured by unnamed interests, suspends her; the inventory ledger goes missing from her desk. Beat: institutional power flexing quietly.

chapters.title: Copies
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Realizing the originals could vanish, she photographs every postcard and hides prints in returned library books across the city. Beat: turning a library into an archive of defiance.

chapters.title: Renny's Daughter
chapters.summary: Adaeze Okafor POV. A retired teacher receives a postcard naming her father's killer; she has waited her whole life for a document, not a rumor. Beat: hope handled carefully so it doesn't break.

chapters.title: The Trust
chapters.summary: Ambrose POV. Board meeting of the Thornbury Charitable Trust, where philanthropy launders guilt; Ambrose moves to liquidate assets ahead of the demolition. Beat: respectability as armor.

chapters.title: What Wendell Remembers
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Childhood memory surfaces: being carried out of the Thornbury house at seven, told never to ask about the wardrobe room. Beat: discovering she was always part of the arrangement.

chapters.title: The Lawyer Who Kept Copies
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Aldous's old solicitor, dying himself, admits he kept duplicate settlement papers and points her to a safe-deposit box. Beat: the law's own guilty archive.

chapters.title: Box 214
chapters.summary: Wendell and Adaeze POV alternating. They open the deposit box together: safety reports, a payout ledger, and a letter Aldous wrote but never sent — apologizing to no one. Beat: evidence without absolution.

chapters.title: Ambrose Learns About Box 214
chapters.summary: Ambrose POV. His investigator reports the breach; Ambrose escalates from money to menace, arranging a break-in at Wendell's apartment. Beat: fear changing the stakes.

chapters.title: The Break-In
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Her home is searched, nothing stolen — a message, not a theft. She sleeps at the library among the shelves. Beat: vulnerability met with stubbornness.

chapters.title: Quentin's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Quentin POV. Recorded at Wendell's request, he narrates the cover-up in full detail, naming every accomplice still living. Beat: relief and dread in the same breath.

chapters.title: Quentin's Confession, Part Two
chapters.summary: Quentin POV. He confesses his own crime: he helped bury Renny's death and took his share of the silence for forty years. Beat: the corrupter corrupted by himself.

chapters.title: The Family Summons Her
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. A formal meeting at the estate: aunt, cousins, lawyers. They offer restitution to Adaeze in exchange for the postcards and her silence. Beat: justice priced like real estate.

chapters.title: Adaeze Decides
chapters.summary: Adaeze POV. Offered money her father never saw, she refuses to trade the record for the check: 'You don't buy back a man.' Beat: dignity as refusal.

chapters.title: Leak
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. A journalist friend runs the story; the city wakes up to the Thornbury name overnight. Beat: the sleeping city finally reading its mail.

chapters.title: Demolition Permit Suspended
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Public pressure freezes the house's demolition; Wendell gets legal standing as finder of the documents. Beat: small victories feeling enormous.

chapters.title: Ambrose Unravels
chapters.summary: Ambrose POV. The trust's board turns on him; he burns papers in the estate fireplace and realizes his father's system survives only if no one tells the truth — and everyone is telling it now. Beat: power discovering it was only ever agreement.

chapters.title: The Last Recipient
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. She deciphers the final unmailed postcard: it is addressed to her, dated the year of her birth. Beat: the story turning inward.

chapters.title: To Wendell, From Quentin
chapters.summary: Quentin POV. The postcard's text: he watched her as a child, saw Aldous begin arranging her life too, and started writing to her the day she was born — forty years of letters to the one person who might finish what he couldn't. Beat: love expressed as evidence.

chapters.title: What the Law Can Do
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Prosecutors open a case, but statutes have expired; the law can shame but not sentence. Wendell confronts the limits of legal justice. Beat: righteous frustration.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Courtroom
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The city responds where courts can't: the trust dissolves, the family name comes off the library wing, dockworkers hold a memorial for Renny. Beat: communal reckoning.

chapters.title: Ambrose at the Door
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Ambrose arrives broken, asking whether reading the postcards made her happy. She answers honestly: no — necessary, not happy. Beat: mercy without reconciliation.

chapters.title: Quentin Stops Eating
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Quentin declines treatment, saying the mail has been delivered. Wendell rages at him for leaving before the end of the story. Beat: anger as a form of love.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. In his care-home room, she reads all forty years of postcards aloud to Quentin over three nights, including the ones about him. Beat: witness as the last sacrament.

chapters.title: The Final Postcard
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. On the last night she reads her own card; Quentin dies before dawn, having heard everything. Beat: release.

chapters.title: The House Comes Down
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. The demolition proceeds at last; Wendell watches from the street as the wardrobe room opens to the sky. Beat: endings that are also exposures.

chapters.title: New Cataloguing Rules
chapters.summary: Wendell POV. Back at the Halcyon Branch, she starts a public collection: undelivered letters, donated anonymously, readable by anyone. Beat: turning private silence into shared record.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Wendell POV, closing. She writes the final entry in her inventory ledger — no longer a list of unsaid things, but a receipt for what was said. She mails one postcard of her own, to no address, trusting the city to deliver it. Beat: peace earned, not granted.
